title: SwingTree Icon Caching
narrative:
SwingTree does a lot of heavy lifting for
    you when it comes to image asset management.
    It can load, instantiate, cache and unload
    image resources for you fully automatically.

    This is possible through instances of the `IconDeclaration`,
    which is a meta-data holder that can tell you where and
    how to obtain an image.
    Typically, this is a path to a png/jpg/svg but it
    may also be an SVG string...
    Instead of loading and instantiating `ImageIcon`s yourself,
    you only need to create a declaration pointing to the resource:

    `var cancel = IconDeclaration.of(path/to/cancel.svg);`

    You can then pass this declaration to a SwingTree GUI,
    and the heavy lifting will be done under the hood for you.
    This is especially powerful because SwingTree uses these icon
    declarations as weak cache keys for icons. So when you no longer
    need an icon, you simply get rid of a strong reference to an icon
    declaration! Under the hood these `IconDeclaration`s are also pooled,
    so you can create and hold them in multiple places of your project
    with the guarantee that the cache will be hit and not cleared prematurely.

features.id: SwingTree maintains a resourceful and robust image cache.

extraInfo:
SwingTree has a weak hash map in its library
            context object which uses `IconDeclaration`s as keys.
            Since these icon declarations are automatically pooled
            when created through factory methods like `IconDeclaration.of(..)`
            the cache is both reliable in terms of hit rate, while also
            being resourceful, since unused entries get cleared automatically.

blocks.text: First we clear the library context so that there is no state leftover from other tests:
We create a bunch of different icon declarations.
code: var icon5 = IconDeclaration.ofSvg("<svg width=\"24\" height=\"24\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\"><circle cx=\"8\" cy=\"8\" r=\"6\" fill=\"red\"/></svg>")

blocks.text: Initially the cache is empty!
We use the icons in various ways.
The cache now contains 5 entries, which are our icons!
We reuse the icons...
The cache does not increase in size because icons are reused.
We set all the usages to `null`...
The cache still full, since we hold on to the declarations:
We replace the existing declarations with the same contents:
code: icon5 = IconDeclaration.ofSvg("<svg width=\"24\" height=\"24\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\"><circle cx=\"8\" cy=\"8\" r=\"6\" fill=\"red\"/></svg>")

blocks.text: The cache is still not cleared, since we are still holding on to the same (pooled) declarations!
We set the first icon declaration to `null` and wait...
The cache finally shrinks by 1:
We set the second icon declaration to `null` and wait...
The cache shrinks again:
We do the third icon declaration...
The cache got smaller again:
We do the fourth icon declaration...
Only one icon left:
We finally clear the last icon declaration...
The cache is empty again!

features.id: A component styled with an inline SVG keeps that SVG parsed for as long as it lives.

extraInfo:
The feature above holds every `IconDeclaration` in a local variable, which is one
            way to use the icon cache but not the common one. A style is far more often written
            like this:

            `UI.panel().withStyle( it -> it.image( img -> img.svg(SOME_SVG_STRING) ) )`

            Here the caller never sees a declaration at all. One is created inside `svg(..)`,
            used to look the icon up, and dropped again -- and since the icon cache is keyed
            *weakly* by declarations, there would then be nothing left in the world to keep the
            entry alive. The parsed SVG document would be thrown away by the very next garbage
            collection, and the next repaint of that component would have to parse the XML all
            over again. On a window which repaints continuously that is a re-parse roughly
            every second, forever.

            So a style which resolved an icon has to hold on to the declaration it resolved it
            from. The scenario below pins that down from the outside: nothing but the styled
            component itself refers to the icon, the garbage collector is then given every
            chance to run, and the icon must still be the one that was parsed at the start.

            The second half is just as important as the first: once the component is gone, the
            entry has to go too. An icon cache that never lets go is not a fix, it is a leak.

blocks.text: A clean library context, so that no icon from another feature is in the cache.
An SVG document in a plain string. Note that a string is not a declaration and keeps nothing alive.
code: var svg = "<svg width=\"24\" height=\"24\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\"><rect x=\"2\" y=\"2\" width=\"12\" height=\"12\" fill=\"blue\"/></svg>"

blocks.text: The cache starts out empty.
We style a panel with that SVG, without ever holding an icon declaration ourselves.
code: var panel = UI.panel().withStyle( it -> it.image( img -> img.svg(svg) ) ).get(JPanel)

blocks.text: The SVG was parsed once and put into the cache.
We remember which icon that produced, and then let the garbage collector run.

The entry survived, because the panel we are still holding refers to the
            declaration it was resolved from.
Asking for the icon again hands back the very same object, so nothing was parsed a second time.
We now drop the panel, which leaves nothing in the world referring to that SVG.
The cache lets go of it, exactly as a weakly keyed cache should.
